chapter_theme: The ten that people do not blame: inborn temper in the untrained, the lowly's lack of eminence, the difficulty of great things and the esteem of rare ones, an uncompletable shortfall, an unjust king (by one living in his land), good kin's omissions, a strange land's customs, the poor man's lack of generosity, and the conduct of the small.

21.reading: People of sense do not fault those who have no binding discipline for the nature they were born with.
21.nuance: யாப்பு is literally a binding or tie; here most likely the binding of training or restraint, so the native temper of the untrained is excused as nature, not chosen fault. It could also mean those with no tie of kin or allegiance. Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten and is printed with this verse.

items.claim: the inborn disposition of those who lack restraint is not held against them

22.reading: People of sense do not fault those of no eminence for lacking the qualities of the eminent.
22.nuance: The line mirrors 21: a lack (மீப்பு இல்லோர்) and a quality (மீக்குணம்). மீக்குணம் can be the higher virtues one should not demand of the lowly, or an overbearing, upward-reaching temper one should not grudge them; a third reading takes மீப்பு இல்லோர் as those with no one above them, whose haughtiness is not blamed. The sense cannot be fixed from the line alone.

items.claim: those without high standing are not blamed with respect to lofty qualities

23.reading: People of sense do not complain that a great thing is hard to come by.
23.nuance: 23 and 24 are a chiasm: பெருமை and அருமை change places, so greatness and rarity are made to entail each other.

items.claim: the difficulty of what has greatness is not a ground of blame

24.reading: People of sense do not grudge the high esteem in which a rare thing is held.
24.nuance: Read with 23: the price of a rare thing and the difficulty of a great one are both accepted as following from what the thing is.

items.claim: the greatness ascribed to what is rare is not blamed

25.reading: People of sense do not blame a deed that falls short because it could not be carried through in full.
25.nuance: குறைவினை can be a work left short or a small task; நிறையச் செய்யா says only that it was not done fully, not why. The line excuses the shortfall, not idleness, on the most natural reading.

items.claim: a deficient work left uncompleted is not censured

26.reading: Those who live in the country of a king who keeps no justice do not openly censure him.
26.nuance: இருந்து is a participle attached to the predicate, so the most natural reading is prudence: one who lives there does not speak against the king. Another reading is that people are not blamed for staying on in such a land. Either way the line counsels the subject, not the king.
26.domain_note: a subject living under an unjust king

items.claim: dwelling in an unjust king's land, one does not voice blame

27.reading: People of sense do not blame good kinsfolk for failing to do what they ought to have done.
27.nuance: The excuse is for good kin (நற்கேளிர்) and for omission (செய்யாமை), not for harm done; the adjective limits the forbearance.

items.claim: the omission of what good kin should have done is not held against them

28.reading: People of sense do not find fault with the customary conduct of a country they do not know.
28.nuance: ஆசாரம் is the same word the Acharakkovai uses for its whole code of conduct; here it is tied to a தேசம் and so allowed to differ from place to place. அறியா may mean a land one does not know or whose ways one does not understand.

items.claim: the rule-bound conduct of an unfamiliar land is not condemned

29.reading: People of sense do not blame a poor man for not being open-handed.
29.nuance: The line sets the limit of others' judgment, not the poor man's own duty; it says nothing on whether he should still try to give.

items.claim: a poor man's failure to be generous is not a fault charged to him

30.reading: Even the most excellent do not blame the conduct of small people.
30.nuance: The உம் in சிறந்தோரும் marks the eminent as the ones most entitled to blame, and so the ones whose restraint matters. சிறியோர் may be the young or the mean in mind.

items.claim: the conduct of the small is not censured even by those who excel

links.note: 24 reverses the terms of 23: the rarity of the great is not blamed, then the greatness of the rare.
links.teaches: The chiasm makes greatness and rarity two faces of one value, so a reader learns that complaining of a thing's cost and grudging its esteem are the same error.

links.note: The Kural says the great accomplish deeds that are hard; the line says the hardness of great things is not to be complained of.
links.teaches: Together they show the link between பெருமை and அருமை from both ends: the great man takes on difficulty, and the onlooker should not resent that great things are difficult.
links.list_adds: Paired with its mirror line 24 in a ten on what is not blamed, it turns the couplet's praise of the great into a rule for those who judge them and their works.

links.note: The Kural grants effort its wage even when the end fails; the line adds that the unfinished work itself is not censured.
links.teaches: The couplet secures the striver's inner reward and the line secures his standing among others, so an honest shortfall costs neither the wage nor the name.
links.list_adds: Set among excuses for nature, poverty and foreign custom, the shortfall becomes one of the things beyond a person's power that the ten exempts from blame, which the couplet on effort does not frame.

links.note: On the reading that the world abandons those who leave a task short, the Kural blames the shortfall that this line excuses.
links.teaches: The pair divides the unfinished task in two: abandoning it in the middle draws the world's blame, while a work that simply could not be done in full does not.
links.list_adds: The ten's predicate puts the onlooker's verdict first, where the couplet speaks to the worker, so the line adds the case the couplet leaves open, a deficiency not chosen.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu counts living under fierce kings of bent sceptre as painful; the line says one living in such a land does not blame the king.
links.teaches: Read together, the pain of misrule and the silence of its subject belong to one situation: the subject suffers it and still holds his tongue, which is prudence, not approval.

links.note: The Kural says having is worse than poverty under a ruler who does no justice; the line says the subject there does not voice blame.
links.teaches: The couplet names what the subject loses under misrule and the line names what he must also give up, the open word against the king, so the cost of a bent sceptre falls on speech as well as property.
links.list_adds: Among the ten's cases of withheld blame it makes silence under an unjust king a rule of the subject's conduct, a side of tyranny the couplet, which speaks of the king's guilt, does not state.

links.note: The Kural reads a friend's hurtful act as folly or great intimacy; the line extends forbearance to good kin who fail to do what they should.
links.teaches: The pair carries the Kural's charity of interpretation from friends' acts to kinsmen's omissions, and keeps its limit: in both, the tie must first be a good one.
links.list_adds: It moves the couplet's rule from friendship to kin and from a wrong done to a duty left undone, and sets it beside excuses for the poor and the small.

links.note: The Kural says understanding lives as the world lives; the line applies that to the customs of an unknown country.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the couplet's conformity turning outward: wisdom not only follows the ways of one's own world but withholds blame from a world whose ways it does not know.
links.list_adds: It names the thing the couplet leaves general, ஆசாரம் of a தேசம், and so makes custom local and the judge's ignorance a reason for restraint.

links.note: Acharakkovai fixes the posture and direction of the meal as ஆசாரம்; the line treats ஆசாரம் as varying by country and not to be faulted where it is unknown.
links.teaches: Holding them together shows that one ethics work treats ஆசாரம் as binding rule while another grants it is a country's custom, so the rule code is local even in the eyes of its own literature.

links.note: The Kural says those who know their duty do not slacken in helping even without means; the line says the poor man who is not generous is not blamed.
links.teaches: The pair separates the ideal from the verdict: the Kural praises the poor man who still helps, while the line forbids others to condemn the one who cannot, so excellence is not made a debt.
links.list_adds: In a ten on withheld blame the line speaks to the onlooker rather than the giver, a standpoint the couplet on ஒப்புரவு never takes.

links.note: The Naladiyar says if poverty makes giving impossible, not begging is worth twice giving; the line says the poor man's lack of generosity is not blamed.
links.teaches: Together they show the poor man's position from both sides: others owe him no reproach for not giving, and he keeps a virtue of his own in not asking.
links.list_adds: The quatrain gives the poor man a substitute duty; the line instead binds the onlooker, placing the poor man beside the untrained and the small as people whose shortfall is excused.

links.note: The Kural says greatness hides another's weakness while smallness tells faults; the line says even the excellent do not blame the conduct of the small.
links.teaches: The pair shows greatness proved on the very people who invite contempt: not publishing a fault is hardest and most telling when the faulty are the small.
links.list_adds: Closing a ten of withheld blame, it turns the couplet's portrait of greatness into the last case of a rule, with சிறந்தோரும் marking the eminent as those for whom restraint is due.

source_issues: 21: the frame line that opens every ten (ஆர்கலி யுலகத்து மக்கட் கெல்லாம்) is printed as line 1 of verse 21; the saying itself is line 2.
21 line 2: the other witness (the site text) lacks this line, so the saying of 21 rests on one witness.
